transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-28
Start time (UTC): 16:00
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Miles (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (CTO - Horizon Retail), Marcus Bell (Head of ML Ops), Sofia Ruiz (Finance Director)

Summary:
Horizon Retail is evaluating hosting options (hosted vs dedicated vs private/VPC) for a checkout assistant and real-time product recommendation service. Primary driver is strict budget control while keeping 95th percentile latency under 200ms for checkout paths. Team is interested in per-token economics, batching/caching levers and pilot scope that demonstrates predictable unit cost. Security (SOC2, KMS, residency) and capacity predictability are secondary gating factors.

Topics covered (rough): per-token pricing targets, batching and KV/prefix caching impact, dedicated vs hosted push/pull tradeoffs, pilot sizing and benchmark plan, required security docs.

Transcript body (timestamps intermittent, imperfect transcription typical of call):
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for joining. quick intros? we'll try to keep this tight and focused on cost levers and what a pilot looks like for you.
[00:12] Lena (Horizon CTO): hi it's Lena, I'm the CTO. Marcus is ML ops and Sofia is finance. thanks for doing this. we got a narrow window on budget this quarter so looking for clarity on unit economics.
[00:22] Marcus (ML Ops): yeah we run recommendations + a checkout chat assistant, mostly sub-second interactions, target p95 under 200 ms for checkout. throughput varies, peak around 220 rps during promos.
[00:35] Priya (Redwood SE): got it. with Redwood we usually look at a few levers: per-token list price, batching and continuous batching, KV/prefix caching (to reuse early tokens), and routing to lower-cost model variants for non-critical flows. what target per-token are you thinking?
[00:48] Sofia (Finance): from finance perspective, pilot budget is capped — we can spend up to $12k for a 30-day pilot. want to understand how that maps to tokens and traffic.
[00:58] Lena: also want to know whether dedicated capacity makes sense — we care about predictable throughput during promotions.
[01:06] Jordan: totally. rough rule of thumb — batching + KV cache can cut effective per-token cost substantially for repetitive contexts, sometimes 30-60% depending on cache hit rates. that's a wide range, so we want to anchor with your traffic profile.
[01:20] Marcus: our checkout assistant has a fairly high prefix reuse; cart metadata and user context is often repeated. I imagine KV cache helps a lot there.
[01:28] Priya: yes, KV cache (we sometimes say K-V cash in quick speech) reduces autoregressive compute for tokens that are already in cache — saves GPU cycles for p95 paths. also continuous batching will pack short requests together, the savings depend on arrival pattern.
[01:42] Speaker 6: (inaudible) question — what's the difference in guarantees if we go hosted vs dedicated?
[01:48] Jordan: hosted is fastest to get going and has flexible scaling; you pay per token and we manage autoscaling. dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools, more predictable throughput and lower unit cost once you cross a commit threshold, plus capacity isolation. Private/VPC adds network residency and customer-controlled keys.
[02:05] Sofia: for finance, predictability is key — we prefer a capped monthly spend or committed capacity vs a purely variable per-token bill.
[02:13] Priya: we can structure pilots in a few ways: 1) hosted trial with per-token visibility and a token budget cap (easy, quick), 2) short-term dedicated with a small reserved pool for the pilot to demonstrate baseline throughput and lower per-token, or 3) private deployment if you need KMS/HSM and strict residency — that takes longer.
[02:31] Marcus: what's the normal uplift to latency when you enable batching? we worry about adding latency to checkout.
[02:36] Priya: continuous batching is latency-aware — it waits only microseconds to pack requests. for checkout flows we tune batching thresholds aggressively; if your p95 target is 200 ms we can usually keep within that while still seeing material cost reductions. there's a tradeoff though: higher batching window = lower cost but added queueing latency.
[02:52] Lena: can you give an example mapping budget to tokens? like if we had $12k, how many requests or tokens does that buy?
[02:58] Jordan: ballpark example (these are illustrative): If your effective per-token cost is $0.00025 after cache and batching, $12k buys ~48M tokens. If your average interaction is 300 tokens (prompt+response) that's ~160k interactions. But again, cache can make average effective tokens per call much lower for checkout because prompts share overlap.
[03:18] Sofia: ok that's helpful, but we need hard numbers during pilot.
[03:22] Jordan: agreed — we'll run a benchmark with your sample traffic to produce an empirical unit-econ sheet. I'll include several scenarios: no cache, 30% cache hit, 60% cache hit, and batching windows.
[03:33] Marcus: about model variants — can we fallback to a smaller model for cheap flows? for example, use a 3B-ish model for category browse and a larger one for checkout.
[03:40] Priya: yes, routing by policy is standard. Redwood routing can send critical checkout tokens to a high-performance variant and cheaper flows to smaller models, and we can do automatic fallback if capacity constrained. That helps average cost.
[03:55] Lena: security questions — we need SOC2, KMS support, audit logs, and SSO. can you provide docs?
[04:01] Jordan: yes. we'll share SOC2 and our encryption/KMS integration notes. For private/VPC deployments you keep keys in your KMS and we integrate via mutual TLS.
[04:09] Sofia: timeline: if pilot runs in March we need a contract by mid-March. can you give a short pilot SOW?
[04:16] Jordan: sure. Typical SOW: 30-day pilot, reserved dev capacity or hosted with token cap, defined traffic profile, benchmark run, final unit-econ report and a recommendation whether to move to Dedicated for production. We'll add acceptance criteria (p95 latency, max spend, and quality checks).
[04:31] Marcus: for the benchmark, what do you need from us?
[04:34] Priya: a representative dataset, example prompts, and an endpoint for metric scraping (or we'll instrument ours). Ideally a 24–72 hour traffic trace at different load levels including a promo spike sample.
[04:45] Marcus: we can do that. I'll anonymize and send by next week.
[04:49] Speaker 2: (overlap) do you support token-level cost breakdowns for each route?
[04:53] Jordan: yes, Redwood Console provides token-level breakdowns per route/model and per-token latency and cost. That helps finance reconcile the bill.
[05:02] Sofia: what about quantization/precision? do smaller quantized models significantly drop quality for checkout intent parsing?
[05:08] Priya: quantization can reduce GPU memory and cost; for many tasks 4-bit quant is fine but you need to evaluate quality. For checkout intent parsing often 4-bit is acceptable; we'll include a QC verification set in the benchmark.
[05:22] Lena: and during Black Friday we need burst capacity — does a dedicated pool let us burst more reliably?
[05:28] Jordan: dedicated pools can be configured with burst capacity or an autoscale buffer. The commercial part is sizing the reserved commit so peak is covered. Otherwise hosted will autoscale but can be less predictable cost-wise.
[05:40] Marcus: any hidden costs we should watch for? network egress for private, storage for cached prompts?
[05:45] Jordan: good point — network egress in private deployments and long-term KV store retention can add cost; we'll call those out separately in the pilot pricing doc.
[05:52] Sofia: can we do a blended pricing example: reserved + per-token overage?
[05:56] Jordan: yes, that's common: a commit that covers baseline throughput and a per-token or per-minute overage for spikes. We'll model both in the spreadsheet.
[06:05] Lena: sounds good. can you include a variant that shows shifting non-critical traffic to a cheaper region or model to save cost?
[06:11] Priya: yup — routing by region/model tier is doable, and we'll show the economics.
[06:15] Jordan: quick recap of deliverables: Jordan sends pilot pricing + scenarios; Priya schedules benchmark and gives run README; Horizon provides traffic traces and SLOs; Redwood shares SOC2/KMS links. We'll aim for pilot start in the first half of March.
[06:30] Sofia: great. last question — do you have a sample pilot invoice template? finance wants to see how charges will appear.
[06:36] Jordan: yes we'll include a sample invoice layout and a short SOW.
[06:40] Lena: awesome, thanks.
[06:42] Jordan: thanks all. we'll follow up by email with the spreadsheet and scheduling links.

End of call.
